title: The Fox Who Hid Warm Things
creature: An arctic fox who buries anything warm
summary: The lost gloves are all in one place, and it is not a hiding place. It is a store.

chapters.title: What Goes Missing
chapters.text: Things go missing at Skálanes and everybody knows which things. Not tools. Not keys, not phones, not the small metal objects that vanish in every house on earth. What goes missing at Skálanes, and has gone missing for as long as anybody can produce a complaint about it, is anything made of wool. Gloves, principally. Ari's mother reckons the household has lost somewhere between four and nine gloves a year since he was born, which over twelve years is a number she does not like saying out loud. There is a box in the porch at Skálanes with about thirty single gloves in it. Every farm on that road has one. It is understood in that part of Iceland that you do not throw away a widowed glove, because the other one might come back, and about one in six of them does — turning up in a ditch in the spring, or under a fence, or once, memorably, folded on a gatepost. Also: a hat off a fence post. Three pairs of socks off the line, always the socks and never the shirts. The lining out of a boot. Half a sheepskin that was under the back door for people to wipe their feet on and that was there on a Tuesday and gone on a Wednesday, and which weighed about four kilos. The village had a theory and the theory was the wind, which is not a stupid theory in a place where the wind takes roofs. It accounted for most of it. Anything on a line, anything on a wall, anything left on the seat of the quad — the wind at Skálanes will take all of that and has taken a trampoline. Nobody had ever had to look any further, because the wind is a complete explanation that requires no thought and is right about eight times out of ten. Ari stopped believing it at eleven for a reason that had nothing to do with anything clever. He watched a glove go. It was on the wall by the byre, in April, in a dead calm — the first properly still day of that year, so still that the smoke from the Hansdóttir chimney was going straight up — and he was thirty metres away doing something with a bucket, and he looked up because of the movement, and there was a glove going along the top of the wall about a foot above the stone. Under it, going at a fast trot with her head up and the glove in her teeth, was a fox. She was in the blue phase — grey-brown in summer, small, low, with the short round ears they have — and she was not skulking. She went along the base of that wall in full daylight thirty metres from a boy with a bucket at a pace that said she had somewhere to be and had done this route a great many times. Ari stood there with the bucket until she was out of sight, which took about forty seconds, and then went in and said nothing to anybody for the rest of the day.

chapters.title: The Store
chapters.text: He found the cache in the June and it took him two months and a great deal of walking, and the method was not sophisticated: he watched, and he wrote down the direction, and he did that eleven times over eight weeks. Watching is most of it and watching is dull. He sat on the wall by the byre with a book he was not reading for something in the region of forty hours across that spring, and he saw a fox six times, and only three of those were carrying anything. The other five directions came from his mother and from the Hansdóttir boy, who both agreed to tell him and who both, he is fairly sure, thought he was wasting a summer. Everything went north-east. The cache is under a slab on the seaward side of the ridge, about two kilometres from the last house, in a place with no particular features that Ari has ever been able to describe to anybody without drawing a map. He got the slab up with a fence post and he sat back on his heels and looked at it for a long time. There were, by his count that afternoon, ninety-four items. He counted them twice, out on the grass, in two rows, and then put every single one back before he left, which took the better part of an hour and which he has always been glad about. Gloves: forty-one, not one of them a pair. Socks: nineteen. Four hats. The boot lining. A great deal of raw sheep's wool of the kind that comes off a fence in June and that nobody would ever miss. Two lengths of knitting still on the needles, which he took home and which turned out to have gone from a windowsill in 2021 and which caused, when he produced them, the largest reaction of the entire summer. And the sheepskin, folded, at the back, four kilos of it, dragged two kilometres uphill by an animal that weighs three and a half. It was dry. That is the thing that undid him. It is under a slab on a seaward ridge in Iceland and there is drainage under it that Ari has never been able to work out, and the whole of it was dry and none of it was chewed. Nothing had been eaten. Nothing had been shredded for bedding. It was not a nest — there was no den within sixty metres and he checked properly, with a torch, over two visits. It was a store, and it had been sorted. He has been back perhaps sixty times since and the number goes up and down. The highest he has counted is a hundred and forty-one, in the September he was seventeen. The lowest was thirty-eight, one April, after a winter that everybody on that coast remembers. That April is the only real evidence he has that any of it is for anything. Fifty-odd items of wool went out of that cache between October and March and none of it was in the ditches and none of it came home. The wool was at the back and the manufactured things were at the front and the four hats were together, and Ari has never once been able to decide whether that last observation is real or whether he is a person who found ninety-four objects under a rock and wanted them to mean something.

chapters.title: Why
chapters.text: The dull explanation is right and Ari has known it since he was about fourteen. Arctic foxes cache. It is one of the most thoroughly documented things they do. A fox on a seabird cliff will take and bury hundreds of eggs in a season — there is a study from Wrangel Island with a number over nine hundred — and they bury them one at a time, in scattered places, and they remember where. They cache anything that might be worth having later. In a hard winter a cached egg from July is the difference. The behaviour is not fussy about what the thing is; it is triggered by *surplus*, and a fox that finds something it cannot use now and might use later will take it and put it somewhere. Wool smells of sheep and of people and of lanolin, which is to say it smells strongly of something that was recently alive. And a fox does not have a category for *glove*. It has a category for *smells of animal, portable, not currently useful*, and a hand-knitted mitten off a windowsill fits that description exactly and so does an egg. That is the whole of it. There is no puzzle. Every wildlife biologist Ari has ever mentioned it to has said essentially the same four sentences, cheerfully, and one of them said it was a nice example and asked for photographs. What none of them accounted for, and what Ari has stopped raising because it makes him sound like a person with a theory, is the sorting. And the fact that in twelve years and something over three hundred items, not one thing that was not warm has ever been in that cache. No plastic. No paper. No rope, and there is rope all over that farm. No leather that had not been lined. He has tested it, which he thinks is the only genuinely scientific thing he has ever done. At fifteen he put four objects out on the wall by the byre on the same evening, all about the same size and weight: a woollen sock, a nylon sock, a strip of tarpaulin, and a length of baler twine. The woollen sock went that night. The other three were on the wall a week later and he brought them in. He did it again the following spring with the same result and a fifth object, a fleece hat, which also went. That is a sample of two trials and he is aware that this would not get past anybody.

chapters.title: The Blue One
chapters.text: He took one thing out of it and put four things in, and that is the arrangement he has kept for eleven years. The thing he took was a mitten. It was blue and it was hand-knitted with a pattern round the cuff in a way that nobody in Iceland does by accident, and it had belonged to his grandmother, and it had gone off a windowsill in the November of 2019 about four months before she died. Its pair was in a drawer in his mother's room. It had been in that drawer for six years because you do not throw away one of a pair when the person who made both is gone, and Ari had watched his mother open that drawer perhaps a hundred times and not say anything. He knew the pattern round the cuff before he had the whole mitten out from under the slab. There is a way of turning the eight-pointed rose at the wrist that his grandmother did and that is slightly wrong, and every person in that family can identify it across a room. He carried it down the ridge inside his coat and he did not tell anybody for two days, and then he put it on the kitchen table. His mother picked it up and turned it over and said, "Where." He told her. All of it — the eight weeks of watching, the directions, the slab, the ninety-four things, the sheepskin folded at the back. She listened the whole way through and then she went and got the other one and put the two of them together on the table, and neither of them said anything for a while. It is not a good story about a woman being given something back. His mother did not cry and did not thank him particularly. She turned the recovered one inside out, looked at the wrist, said that the tension had gone at the end and that his grandmother's hands had been bad by then, and put both of them in the drawer. They are still in the drawer. Nobody wears them. Ari has thought about that and has concluded that a pair in a drawer is a different object from a single in a drawer, and that this was the whole of what he had brought home. Then she said: "What did you leave?" He had not left anything. It had not occurred to him. He went up the next weekend with an old fleece cut into four pieces and put them under the slab, and he has done something similar three or four times a year ever since — offcuts, mostly, and the wool that comes off the fence in June that he now collects on purpose. He does not know whether it makes any difference to anything. He is aware that a fox does not have gratitude and does not keep accounts and would take the fleece whether he had ever found the cache or not. Ari is twenty-three and works on the boats and comes home in the winter. The gloves still go. His mother still loses between four and nine a year and complains about it in exactly the same words, and Ari has never once suggested that she stop. He has told her where they are. She knows. She has never been up there and has never asked to go, and once, when he offered to take her, she said that it was two kilometres and that she had a farm to run and that if a fox wanted her gloves it was welcome to them. Ari thinks she means it and also thinks she would rather they were somewhere than nowhere.
